### What “triangulation metrics” actually mean In most contexts—whether you’re working with geographic information systems (GIS), computer‑graphics meshes, or even statistical models—**triangulation** is the process of breaking a space into triangles (or tetrahedra in 3‑D). Because the quality of that break‑up matters a lot, we use **metrics** to quantify how good the triangulation is. These metrics let you: | Domain | Typical triangulation problem | Common metrics | Why it matters | |--------|------------------------------|----------------|----------------| | **Geodesy / Surveying** | Determining a point’s latitude/longitude from angles measured at known stations | • **Positional error** (difference between computed and true coordinates)
• **Root‑mean‑square (RMS) error**
• **Maximum error** | Ensures that the network of survey stations gives you accurate maps and legal boundaries. | | **GIS / Remote sensing** | Creating a digital elevation model (DEM) from LiDAR or photogrammetry points | • **Mean absolute error (MAE)**
• **Standard deviation of residuals**
• **Coverage percentage** (how much of the area is represented) | Determines how reliable the terrain model is for flood modeling, infrastructure planning, etc. | | **Computer graphics / Finite‑element analysis** | Meshing a surface or volume for rendering or simulation | • **Aspect ratio** (ratio of longest to shortest edge)
• **Minimum/maximum angle** (to avoid skinny triangles)
• **Edge length distribution**
• **Element quality factor** (e.g., scaled Jacobian) | Affects rendering speed, numerical stability, and accuracy of simulations. | | **Statistical / Machine‑learning** | Using triangulation to interpolate or approximate a function over a domain | • **Interpolation error** (difference between predicted and actual values)
• **Cross‑validation score**
• **Number of triangles per unit area** | Helps decide whether the model is over‑ or under‑fitting. | --- ### How the metrics are calculated 1. **Collect ground truth** – For positional problems, you need a set of reference points whose true coordinates are known. 2. **Compute the triangulation** – Run your algorithm (e.g., Delaunay, constrained Delaunay, or a custom mesh generator). 3. **Measure errors** – For each point, compute the difference between its triangulated coordinate and the ground truth. 4. **Aggregate** – Take statistics (mean, RMS, max) across all points. 5. **Report** – Present the results in tables, plots, or dashboards. --- ### Why you’d want to expose these metrics via an API The function you mentioned (`requests_get`) pulls “products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days.” If you expose **triangulation metrics** through that same endpoint, you can: * **Track performance over time** – See if newer algorithms reduce error. * **Compare branches** – Identify which branch of your codebase produces the best meshes. * **Trigger alerts** – If error exceeds a threshold, automatically flag the run for review. * **Feed dashboards** – Visualize trends for stakeholders who don’t need raw data but want high‑level insights. --- ### Quick cheat‑sheet of common metrics | Metric | Formula | Interpretation | |--------|---------|----------------| | **Positional error** | \( e_i = \sqrt{(x_i - x_{\text{true}})^2 + (y_i - y_{\text{true}})^2} \) | Distance between computed and true location. | | **RMS error** | \( \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} e_i^2} \) | Average error magnitude. | | **Aspect ratio** | \( \frac{\text{longest edge}}{\text{shortest edge}} \) | Lower is better; avoids skinny triangles. | | **Minimum angle** | Smallest interior angle in a triangle | Avoids angles < 20° for stability. | | **Scaled Jacobian** | \( \min\left(\frac{2A}{ab+bc+ca}\right) \) where \(A\) is area and \(a,b,c\) are edge lengths | 1 is perfect equilateral; lower values indicate poor quality. | --- ### Bottom line Triangulation metrics are the quantitative yardsticks you use to judge how well a triangulation algorithm is doing—whether it’s positioning points accurately, creating a clean mesh for rendering, or interpolating data smoothly. By exposing these metrics through your API, you give users a clear, actionable view of performance and quality, enabling faster iteration and higher confidence in the results.
